reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant genodermatosis caused by germline CYLD mutations predisposing to multiple adnexal tumours
Characteristic tumours are cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas, which may coexist and even collide within a single lesion (spiradenocylindroma)
Cylindromas favour the scalp and may coalesce into disfiguring turban tumours, while trichoepitheliomas cluster on the central face and nasolabial folds
It forms a clinical spectrum with familial cylindromatosis and multiple familial trichoepithelioma, all linked to CYLD
Lesions typically appear from adolescence and increase in number and size through adult life, with female predominance in some kindreds
The CYLD gene encodes a deubiquitinase that negatively regulates NF-kB signalling; its loss promotes adnexal tumorigenesis
Malignant transformation of cylindromas or spiradenomas is uncommon but recognised, so changing lesions warrant biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition arising from germline loss-of-function mutations in the CYLD tumour-suppressor gene, with a somatic second hit inactivating the remaining allele in tumour tissue. CYLD encodes a deubiquitinating enzyme that removes regulatory ubiquitin chains from signalling intermediates, thereby restraining nuclear factor-kappa B and related pro-survival pathways. Loss of this brake enhances cell survival and proliferation in follicular and apocrine/eccrine adnexal structures, generating the syndrome's hallmark cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas. Because the underlying defect is shared, individual lesions can display overlapping or combined histological features, and the same genotype produces the overlapping phenotypes of familial cylindromatosis and multiple trichoepithelioma.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic solitary cylindroma, spiradenoma, or trichoepithelioma
Cowden syndrome and other hamartoma syndromes
Multiple basal cell carcinomas / basal cell naevus syndrome
Nevoid follicular tumours and adnexal hamartomas
additionalInvestigations: Detailed skin examination mapping cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas
Skin biopsy of representative lesions for histological confirmation
CYLD germline genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and enable family counselling
Family history and examination of at-risk relatives
Imaging and surgical planning for extensive confluent scalp disease
Biopsy of any rapidly changing lesion to exclude malignant transformation
redFlags: A rapidly growing, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion suggesting malignant transformation of a cylindroma or spiradenoma
Extensive disfiguring turban-tumour disease with functional impact
New neurological or local symptoms from large or deep tumours
Emergence of aggressive histology on biopsy of a long-standing tumour
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is chronic and progressive with recurring benign tumours that cause cosmetic and functional morbidity and often require repeated surgery; life expectancy is generally normal, but the small risk of malignant transformation necessitates lifelong surveillance.
pitfalls: Treating a patient's tumours as isolated sporadic lesions and missing the hereditary diagnosis
Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening
Overlooking malignant transformation in a long-standing changing lesion
Inadequate excision of confluent scalp tumours leading to recurrence
management: Manage the hallmark cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas with surgical excision of symptomatic, enlarging, or disfiguring lesions, including scalp excision and grafting for confluent turban tumours
Treat smaller or numerous facial lesions with ablative techniques such as carbon-dioxide laser, electrosurgery, or dermabrasion
Undertake lifelong dermatological surveillance and biopsy any rapidly changing lesion to detect malignant transformation
Confirm the diagnosis with skin biopsy and CYLD germline genetic testing
Offer genetic counselling and cascade screening of at-risk relatives given the autosomal dominant inheritance
Provide multidisciplinary care with plastic surgery and psychological support for the cosmetic and functional burden
